items.title: In Pursuit of Ideal Data: Epistemic Enchantment and the Unintended Consequences of Datafying for Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The increasing datafication of work has become a pervasive theme within organizations, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that rely on data and machine learning to generate insights and decisions. Prior research has shown that datafication practices aimed at administrative control and accountability can transform organizations in profound and often unintended ways. Our research moves beyond investigating datafication for administrative purposes to explore how it unfolds when actors intend to extract knowledge through AI predictive modeling. Drawing on a three-year ethnography of a human resources (HR) department introducing AI for candidate screening, we find that datafication expanded far beyond the technology’s initially envisioned scope. We explain this scope expansion by introducing the concept of epistemic enchantment : a collective process through which organizational members become captivated and mobilized by AI’s promise to generate predictive, objective, and continuously improving insights from data, while overlooking the costs and risks involved. Our study reveals how datafication practices can expand endlessly as organizational members, enchanted by AI’s epistemic promises, pursue the notion of ideal data as an ever-desired but never reachable goal.

items.title: Innovations in the gaming experience and the impact of artificial intelligence on communication mechanisms
items.abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on the structure of interaction and communication mechanisms in digital games. Against the background of the rapid development of generative technologies, video games are becoming media platforms in which AI not only provides personalization and scenario adaptation, but also forms new forms of role identity, cognitive engagement and political socialization. The research is based on an interdisciplinary approach combining media theoretical, political-analytical and critical-discursive analysis. Three game projects are considered as an empirical basis, in which AI acts as a media intermediary that sets the framework for the interpretation, control and representation of power. The comparative analysis makes it possible to identify the key functions of AI: from algorithmic selection of meanings to modeling digital subjectivity. It is concluded that AI in games functions as a political and communication actor that transforms the rules of interaction and the architecture of user experience.

items.title: Integrating AI-assisted design thinking in citizenship education: Enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills
items.abstract: This study aims to analyse the implementation of an AI-assisted design thinking learning model in enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills in Citizenship Education programmes. The study employed a qualitative approach involving undergraduate students from several Citizenship Education programmes at universities on Java Island, Indonesia. The learning implementation integrated artificial intelligence (AI) to assist students in exploring information, generating ideas and reflecting on solutions to civic and social issues. Research data were collected through observations of the learning process, analysis of students’ assignment documents, AI-assisted interaction records and group discussions conducted during the implementation of the model. Data were analysed descriptively to identify the dynamics of the learning process at each stage of design thinking. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design thinking encouraged students to engage actively in social problem analysis and problem-solving. During the empathise stage, students identified social issues through digital information exploration, AI use and group discussions, enabling them to understand problems from multiple perspectives. In the define stage, students formulated problems more systematically by identifying causal relationships and the underlying social contexts. The ideate stage encouraged students to generate alternative solutions creatively and collaboratively through group discussions and AI-supported idea development. In the prototype and test stages, students developed solution designs in the form of programmes or simple policy models and evaluated their effectiveness through reflection, feedback and AI-assisted analysis. The study concludes that AI supports, but does not replace, students’ critical reasoning, the quality of which depends on reflective pedagogical design.

items.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence into Architectural Education: An Online Model Proposal for Instructor Training for Studio Courses
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is driving a fundamental paradigm shift in architectural design, transitioning from deterministic drafting to algorithmic curation. While the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector rapidly adopts these tools, academic curricula face a “Techno-Instructional Void.” This gap risks inducing a “Zero Order Thinking State” (ZOTS)—a cognitive passivity rooted in Cognitive Load Theory, where students uncritically accept unbuildable machine hallucinations. To address this, we applied a Design and Development Research (DDR Type 2) methodology to build a conceptual framework. It revolves around the “Twin Houses” andragogy and the “Technical Sealing” protocol. By enforcing “Cognitive Friction,” the framework compels students to validate probabilistic GenAI outputs against ergonomic constants (such as Blondel’s Formula) and safety norms. We intentionally reject automated AI-to-BIM pipelines. Instead, the model turns Building Information Modeling (BIM) into an active Proof-Assistant. Learners have to manually and parametrically rationalize their AI-generated ideas utilizing visual programming APIs (Revit Dynamo, Allplan PythonParts) and IFC 4.3 data schemas for rigorous Rule-Based Checking (RBC). Formal expert validation interviews (n = 5) and empirical observations of Turkish student design cases support this theoretical model. While we initially noted autoethnographic evidence of institutional resistance across certain European academic ecosystems, the model subsequently secured preliminary external support from a leading institution in Germany. Ultimately, this framework provides a structured andragogical approach, equipping instructors to guide students in understanding how probabilistic algorithmic outputs can be systematically translated into buildable tectonic realities when subjected to rigorous deterministic technical validation.

items.title: Inteligencia sin comprensión. Magnifica Humanitas: de las dos ausencias de la máquina y la custodia de la persona
items.abstract: This article examines the central claim of the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2026), namely that artificial intelligence is fundamentally different from human intelligence and that, therefore, the human person requires special protection. Drawing on epistemology, philosophy of mind, and Kantian thought, the author argues that contemporary AI systems are marked by two fundamental limitations: they lack understanding and experience. Although they can generate convincing and useful responses, they do not grasp the conceptual relations that structure human knowledge, nor do they possess the lived experience through which the world acquires meaning. Based on these absences, the article introduces the concept of conversational heteronomy, understood as the gradual replacement of personal judgment by conclusions generated by systems that neither reason nor experience as subjects. The study concludes that the ethical challenge is not to reject artificial intelligence, but to employ it without surrendering the distinctly human capacities to understand, experience, and judge, thereby preserving moral autonomy and human dignity.

items.title: Interdisciplinary Colloquium on Digitalisation of Research: "Why so serious? Generative AI (genAI) in Knowledge-Work from a Text-Workers' Perspective" 2026.10.01 with Janine Gondolf and Clemens Ackerl
items.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) systems have become an integral part of scientific text-producing practice. They can conduct literature-related research, organize content and information, proofread text, and assist with writing itself. Above all, they are credited with reducing workload by taking on or taking over these routine tasks. Drawing on an internal, interdisciplinary KIT-ITAS project that deployed the genAI-supported research assistance system 'Undermind.ai', we demonstrate that the potential to reduce workload is offset by the need to reorganize basic scientific competencies in response to the changing workflow requirements of genAI-assisted knowledge work. GenAI systems produce texts that closely resemble stylistic conventions and appear both well-formed and plausible. However, the closer these texts adhere to researchers’ expectations, the more challenging it becomes to verify their content using established academic methods. This generates higher-order efforts that must be weighed against existing working standards for assessing text-based results. The constant validation and ongoing negotiation of plausibility with the system’s output, both during and beyond the writing process, places additional demands on researchers’ critical competence and judgement. Using genAI in knowledge work thus shifts the focus of familiar textual and intellectual labour practices and procedures away from independent creation and toward the verification of textual output, along with the corresponding demands on epistemic attention, responsibility, authorization, and authority.

items.title: Judgement in the Age of Jev: From Evaluation Scarcity to Evaluation Abundance
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has reduced the cost of producing plausible symbolic artefacts, leading recent organisation scholarship to identify evaluation and discernment as constraints under conditions of production abundance. This perspective examines a further possibility: that machine evaluation itself becomes inexpensive enough to be deployed routinely and at scale. The investigation is prompted by Jev, TypeSafe AI's specialised model for typed probabilistic decisions. TypeSafe explicitly invokes William Stanley Jevons to argue that lower-cost machine intelligence can unlock previously uneconomic uses. Treating this as a technological provocation rather than an established empirical result, the article formulates a conditional Jevons hypothesis for machine evaluation: sufficiently large reductions in the total marginal cost of usable machine evaluation may increase its organisational consumption where latent demand is substantial and complementary costs do not dominate. The article integrates rebound economics with research on cheap prediction, production abundance, machine evaluation, decision allocation, authority, reliance and Executive Judgement to examine this possible scarcity transition. It distinguishes prediction, machine evaluation, organisational judgement and authorisation as functional activities whose costs need not fall together. Evaluations can share evidence, criteria and errors; scale mis-specified rubrics; operate on representations from which consequential qualifications have disappeared; and change practical decision rights through thresholds and exception routing. The resulting research problem is when cheap machine evaluation substitutes for human evaluative work, when it redistributes or creates demands for judgement, and how it affects the grounds available at consequential organisational commitment.

items.title: Key Concepts Regarding the Ethical Implications of Artificial Intelligence: A Review
items.abstract: This study presents a review of relevant literature on key concepts related to the ethical implications of artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the historical evolution, conceptual foundations, classifications, and ethical frameworks. Furthermore, it adopts the Responsible AI Framework, which emphasises fairness, accountability, transparency, and human-centred design as articulated by global institutions such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), United Nations Education Scientific Cultural Organization (UNESCO), and the European Commission. These frameworks were found to integrate ethical theory and policy and governance perspectives. Finally, the concepts reviewed provide the analytical foundation for understanding the ethical implications of AI in public policy decision-making, particularly within the Nigerian context.

items.abstract: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Disease Surveillance and Outbreak Prediction: A Scoping Review Reporting Standards: JBI Scoping Review Methodology and PRISMA-ScR Guidelines 1. Purpose & Rationale Timely detection and accurate prediction of infectious disease threats are paramount for global health security and emergency response. While the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), deep learning, and transformer architectures in public health, a substantial gap remains between high-performing algorithmic models and their operational integration into frontline surveillance systems. The primary purpose of this research is to systematically map, synthesize, and evaluate the current body of literature on AI-enabled infectious disease surveillance. The project establishes a structured functional taxonomy of computational architectures, evaluates their early-warning capability and predictive lead times, and systematically maps the implementation, governance, and structural barriers that prevent these tools from being seamlessly translated into public health policy and routine health system operations. 2. Research Objectives & Specific Questions The project addresses the following primary research question: *What evidence exists regarding the application of artificial intelligence and computational models for infectious disease surveillance, early detection, outbreak prediction, and surveillance optimization, and what implementation challenges influence their operational integration into public health systems? Specific Research Sub-objectives: 1. Algorithmic Classification: Categorize current AI, machine learning, and deep learning architectures (e.g., CNNs, LSTMs, Transformers, Graph Active Learning) deployed across diverse viral and bacterial pathogen threats. 2. Predictive Performance & Lead-Time Analysis:Evaluate empirical metrics (such as AUROC, sensitivity, and lead time in days or weeks) demonstrated by models in early-warning variant detection and outbreak forecasting. 3. Resource Allocation & Health Systems Optimization:** Assess how computational models optimize pass-through surveillance functions, such as diagnostic site selection, laboratory testing workflows, and supply allocation in resource-constrained health settings. 4. Implementation & Governance Bottlenecks:** Identify key structural, data-latency, ethical, and workforce barriers restricting model integration into routine national public health decision-making. 3. Methodological Overview PCC Eligibility Framework: Population: Human populations or simulated population networks impacted by communicable disease threats. Concept: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, sequence transformers, or computational frameworks applied to surveillance, early warning, outbreak forecasting, or surveillance resource allocation. Context:Global public health surveillance systems, encompassing digital infrastructures in high-income settings and health facility frameworks in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Information Sources & Search Strategy: Multi-database searches across PubMed, MEDLINE, and Google Scholar, complemented by grey literature searches of international public health repositories (WHO, CDC, ECDC) and preprint servers (bioRxiv, medRxiv). Screening Governance: Independent title, abstract, and full-text screening conducted by two independent reviewers, with third-reviewer arbitration for consensus. Quality & Risk of Bias Assessment: Methodological quality evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklists and the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). 4. Expected Outcomes & Public Health Impact** 1. Standardized Functional Taxonomy: A multi-domain framework categorizing AI applications across core surveillance functions ranging from early warning genomic variant prioritization topassive digital anomaly detection. 2.Empirical Performance Evidence Base: A synthesized matrix detailing lead-time advantages and accuracy trade-offs across various algorithmic classes and epidemiological data modalities (e.g., genomic sequences, clinical imaging, mobility streams). 3. Implementation & Policy Roadmap: A comprehensive evaluation of operational bottlenecks, providing health ministries and global health organizations with actionable recommendations to bridge the gap between "black-box" model development and field deployment.

items.title: Lifecycle costs of safety instrumented systems in process industries: a systematic literature review
items.abstract: A safety instrumented system (SIS) is an automated system designed to detect and mitigate potential risk of hazardous conditions in industrial processes by taking actions to prevent or mitigate incidents. It is essential because it helps protect people, equipment, and the environment by reducing the risk of accidents in hazardous operations, such as in chemical plants, oil refineries, or power stations. While the primary objective of SIS design is safety, economic considerations, particularly lifecycle cost, play a pivotal role in decision-making during the design phase. Although research efforts exist to incorporate lifecycle cost with safety, the literature is fragmented and lacks a comprehensive lifecycle cost framework. Therefore, a systematic literature review is conducted to uncover safety instrumented systems’ lifecycle cost elements and the decision variables that impact them. The review results lead to a comprehensive and structured cost calculation framework to assess SIS designed to protect a process unit economically. Finally, this study provides perspectives on potential research directions relevant to SIS lifecycle cost, including the impact of systematic failures, cybersecurity integration, the relative weighting of different cost elements, inclusion of risk costs, and various SIS application types.

items.title: MEA: A Reward-Driven Multi-Agent System for Faithful Model Explanations
items.abstract: Recent years have seen the employment of a plethora of machine learning (ML) models in high-stakes domains, but they remain largely opaque to the practitioners who act on their predictions. While post-hoc explanation methods offer a lens into this model behavior, wielding them effectively demands expertise most domain experts lack: navigating high-dimensional outputs, selecting the best explanations, and synthesizing evidence across disparate tools. To this end, we present MEA, a multi-agent framework that removes the explanation knowledge barrier entirely: a Proposer agent selects and configures explanation tools based on the question and modality, while an Actor agent is optimized end-to-end against faithfulness, transforming the outputs into natural language explanations grounded in model behavior across tabular, text, and vision modalities. Further, we introduce diverse question types spanning feature attribution, counterfactual reasoning, and spurious feature detection, each paired with a perturbation-based faithfulness metric. We find that frontier LLMs systematically produce unfaithful explanations. By optimizing against faithfulness rewards augmented with a modality-adaptive penalty, MEA consistently outperforms post hoc explainers, agentic, and closed-source baselines across six datasets, with reward-driven optimization yielding faithfulness gains of +28% (tabular), +21% (text), and +34% (vision) over the untrained backbone. More broadly, our findings suggest that AI agents themselves can serve as a scalable, adaptable interface to ML explainability, opening a path toward natural-language explainability that generalizes beyond the fixed, single-purpose tools that have long defined the field.

items.title: Measuring head motion across deceleration levels in automated driving: Quantifying comfort
items.abstract: Passenger-centred comfort measures are needed to enable adaptive driving styles in automated vehicles, particularly where comfort begins to decrease. This study examined passengers' head motion during automated braking at a crosswalk. Data from thirty-four participants were analysed, who experienced three deceleration levels (−1.5, −2.5, −3.5 m/s 2 ) and two pedestrian visibility conditions, reflecting how quickly the AV braked after the pedestrian appeared, rating comfort respectively. As expected, head pitch and translational acceleration increased with deceleration intensity, while pedestrian visibility had no effect on head motion, even though faster AV responses were previously found more comfortable, suggesting this reflects passengers' judgement of the AV's response rather than head stability. Head-motion measures did not add predictive value beyond vehicle kinematics, likely because comfort ratings were similar across conditions. In this scenario, head-motion mainly reflected physical response to braking rather than subjective evaluation. Future research should test head-motion measures in more complex driving conditions.

items.title: Metacognition in AI-Supported Second Language Learning: A Systematic Review of Constructs, Measures, and Evidence (2016–2026)
items.abstract: Metacognition has informed research on second and foreign language (L2) learning for three decades, while AI tools have supported such learning for nearly as long. Yet, no review has examined how the field conceptualises and measures metacognition under AI mediation. This systematic review identified 60 eligible studies published between 2016 and May 2026. Each study was coded on fourteen dimensions anchored in established taxonomies and appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Only four eligible studies fall within the pre-ChatGPT portion of the review window, from January 2016 to November 2022; 56 were published during the subsequent three and a half years. Three findings emerge. First, measurement is narrowly concentrated: 98% of the 56 post-ChatGPT studies measured self-reported metacognitive regulation, and 66% relied on self-report alone. Only one study in the full corpus measured metacognitive accuracy. Five post-ChatGPT studies combined an AI-absent comparison with process-level data, and only one of these also measured judgement accuracy. Second, 41% of post-ChatGPT studies used tools that combined two or more functional orientations within a single interface, a configuration not represented by the field’s inherited four-category taxonomy of AI applications. Third, none of the 18 contrast-based studies assigned the regulatory operation to the system in place of the learner. In every design that specified the division of labour, the learner retained that operation; three designs did not specify it. The condition most in need of testing therefore remains untested. Reported findings skew positive, but correlational and qualitative designs account for a disproportionate share of that evidence. The review concludes with a research agenda centred on calibration and process data.

items.title: Mitigating Social Sycophancy via Pluralistic Preference Optimization
items.abstract: Personal advice, including relationship advice, now ranks among the most common uses of generative AI. But language models (LMs) exhibit sycophancy: they affirm users much more often than humans do, which can make people overconfident and less willing to repair their relationships after a conflict. Prior work on mitigating sycophancy has focused on factual settings where a response can be checked against a ground truth answer, while mitigations for social sycophancy (e.g., personal advice, where there is no ground truth) have relied on simple prompting and post-training methods with limited effectiveness. Our insight is that social sycophancy occurs in part because LMs overly center on the user and fail to consider the perspectives of other stakeholders impacted by the user's behavior. To address this problem we propose Pluralistic Preference Optimization (PlurPO): given inputs describing interpersonal conflicts, the LM identifies and simulates the relevant stakeholders, and is then trained to prefer and generate responses acceptable to all stakeholders. PlurPO uses only signals the model produces about its own outputs, without ground-truth labels. PlurPO substantially reduces social sycophancy across four datasets and four model families compared to prior methods. For example, on statements of intent to cause harm, where the users' actions should not be endorsed, PlurPO reduces the endorsement rate by 89% on average across four models. On general advice questions, where the target is to match the endorsement rate of human responses, it closes the gap by more than half, from 17.8% to 8.0% on average. The preference dataset constructed by PlurPO for an 8B model also effectively transfers to mitigating sycophancy in a larger (32B) model. Our results indicate that social sycophancy can be reduced by leveraging a model's own capabilities to simulate a plurality of relevant perspectives.

items.title: Motivational Factors in Interdisciplinary Design Collaboration
items.abstract: This study investigates design collaborations in interdisciplinary work settings, where actors from product design, product development, product management, marketing, production, purchasing, and quality units participate in product design processes, with the aim of contributing to both its theoretical understanding and effective management. By bridging research on design collaboration with motivational theory, the study argues that motivation constitutes a critical yet underexplored dimension of interdisciplinary design collaborations. Adopting an interpretivist approach, the research explores the experiences of twenty-five experts from diverse disciplines through semi-structured interviews. The findings identify three sets of motivational factors: (1) design-specific intrinsic motivational factors of collaboration—belief in the project, continuous progress, and continuous learning; (2) relational factors as distinct motivational drivers through constructive conflict and a sense of “we”; and (3) extrinsic factors that condition rather than generate motivation by shaping the context of collaboration. This article proposes a layered model in which intrinsic, relational, and extrinsic factors interact dynamically to sustain collaborative engagement.

items.title: Multi-Hazard Graph Artificial Intelligence for Infrastructure Resilience Screening in Romania: Integrating Ground Motion, Earth Observation, Hazard Exposure and Network Topology
items.abstract: Natural hazards can disrupt transport infrastructure through spatially heterogeneous flooding, seismic shaking, terrain conditions, and observed ground motion, while local exposure alone does not determine system-wide consequences. This study develops a reproducible multi-hazard Graph Artificial Intelligence framework for infrastructure resilience screening on the Romanian strategic road network. A frozen attributed line graph combines network topology with European land-cover, terrain, seismic, flood, and ground-motion evidence, and an independent disruption simulator provides continuous resilience-loss targets. GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT were trained under a leakage-controlled three-seed protocol. On the blind 194-scenario PRIMARY TEST, ensemble RMSE/R2 were 0.013343/0.997104 for GCN, 0.013978/0.996822 for GraphSAGE, and 0.015830/0.995924 for GAT. A fresh GCN branch achieved RMSE/R2 = 0.018230/0.995852 on 111 component-disjoint cases and 0.010468/0.991654 on 256 severity-specific held-out cases. On 208 predefined external anchors held out from Graph-AI fitting and selection, GAT attained the lowest ensemble RMSE (0.021620; R2 = 0.975065), while seismic-only transfer remained weak (n = 10; R2 = 0.251–0.386). A frozen six-family GCN ablation (18 checkpoints; 194 matched test scenarios) found RMSE = 0.026175 after seismic feature omission versus 0.013343 for the full-input GCN; this is simulator-specific sensitivity, not causal hazard attribution. The results support accurate emulation of the frozen simulator and transfer-aware screening, not structural safety certification. The model outputs are simulator-based rather than observed disruption outcomes; neither an end-to-end simulator-to-GNN speedup nor calibrated prediction intervals are established by the present evaluation.

items.title: Navigating AI Integration in Final Project Supervision: Academic Integrity, Challenges, and Best Practices
items.abstract: Abstract: This study examines the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the thesis supervision process for students in the Islamic Communication and Broadcasting Study Program at Sulthan Thaha Saifuddin State Islamic University (UIN) Jambi. Employing a qualitative approach, the study involved in-depth interviews with 10 students who were actively completing their undergraduate theses during the 2025/2026 academic year and five thesis supervisors. The findings indicate that the integration of AI provides various benefits, including increased efficiency, more personalized guidance, and improved accessibility to academic references. Students reported that AI accelerated the thesis revision process by providing real-time feedback and recommendations for relevant literature. Meanwhile, lecturers experienced a reduced administrative workload through the automation of routine tasks, allowing them to focus more on providing guidance on conceptual and methodological aspects. The recommendations emphasize the importance of institutional policies to enhance technology training and develop digital infrastructure for academic staff and students. Thus, AI can be effectively integrated to support the thesis supervision process and help students achieve their academic potential more optimally. The main limitation of this study lies in its limited sample size, which prevents the findings from being statistically generalized. items.title: NEP 2020 and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Teaching, Learning, and Assessment in Higher Education
items.abstract: Abstract India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 articulates an ambitious vision for the comprehensive reform of higher education, foregrounding technology integration, multidisciplinary learning, and learner-centred pedagogy as central pillars. Concurrently, the global proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) across educational domains has prompted serious scholarly and policy-level engagement with its transformative potential and inherent risks. This paper presents a critical analysis of the intersection between NEP 2020 and AI-driven transformation in three core dimensions of higher education: teaching, learning, and assessment. Drawing upon verified policy documents, systematic reviews, and empirical studies published by reputable international bodies and journals between 2016 and 2025, the paper examines how NEP 2020’s policy architecture creates both affordances and constraints for AI adoption. The analysis reveals that while the policy’s emphasis on digital infrastructure, personalised learning, and continuous assessment aligns substantively with global AI-in-education trajectories, significant challenges persist regarding equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, and assessment integrity. The paper argues that realising NEP 2020’s AI-enabled vision demands a critical, context-sensitive implementation strategy that moves beyond techno-optimism toward principled, evidence-informed integration.

items.title: Occupational Hazards and Utilization of Personal Protective Devices Among Motorcycle Riders in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Motorcycle riders face numerous occupational risks as a result of their exposure to road traffic accidents, environmental conditions, and ergonomic difficulties. This study looked at the use of personal protective equipment and occupational hazards by motorcycle riders in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State. Five objectives, five research questions, and two hypotheses were developed and tested to a significance level of 0.05. With a population of 8,595 motorcyclists in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State, and a sample size of 756 motorcyclists from Rivers West's various local governments, the study employed a descriptive cross-sectional survey design. The reliability coefficient of the self-structured questionnaire that was used for data collection was 0.91, and it was validated by three professors in the department of Human Kinetics, Health, and Safety Education. According to the study's findings, the result demonstrated that motorcyclists were particularly susceptible to physical danger (3.06 0.48). The findings of this study are to be expected because riders are exposed to numerous physically hazardous factors while riding. There was a negative correlation because when riders use personal protective devices like nose masks, eye goggles, and protective clothing, they are less likely to be exposed to physical hazards. When riders use PPD, they are more likely to be exposed to more hazards. It was recommended among others that management of road transport workers should put necessary laws to enforce the utilization of personal protective devices like eye goggle, nose masks, reflective and helmet by drivers or riders to reduce exposure to physical hazards and accidents among motorcyclists, the national union of road transport workers NURTW through their various bodies in rural and urban areas should establish regulatory personnel’s to ensure that there is strict compliance to safety by putting on the necessary protective devices by drivers/riders and fine should be paid for those that fail to comply.

items.title: Organisational Best Practices for AI Accountability and Acceptance
items.abstract: The introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into policing comes with some concerns and challenges: concerns from the public, and indeed police leaders, about the nature of its usage in a context of already declining trust and confidence in policing, and amongst staff concerned about changes to working practices and even job security. The implementation of AI into (forces) organisations must therefore come with comprehensive governance and accountability structures and practices to ensure these concerns are considered and addressed, allowing for the effectiveness and efficiency benefits of AI to flourish alongside sustained—or hopefully improving—public trust and confidence levels. This chapter will highlight, discuss and recommend organisational best practices that should be considered by organisations to help them effectively develop or deploy AI systems across a range of operational use cases.
